title: The Tacky Ten
author: Stuart Jr., Dave
summary: Stuart presents the Tacky Ten, a one-page reference distilled from Kearney et al.'s 1991 research on teacher behaviors that damage student-perceived credibility. The list names ten behaviors — including humiliating students, acting condescendingly, using sarcasm, and grading slowly — that are common yet credibility-corrosive. Stuart annotates five items with practical nuance, noting that harm is contextual: moving test dates is problematic only when habitual or poorly managed, while condescension is especially damaging with adolescents, who are developmentally hypersensitive to it. He frames sarcasm as a structural classroom risk because its ambiguity guarantees that some students will misread it, causing needless alienation. The article closes by recommending the Tacky Ten as a PLC discussion protocol, observing that honest teachers will find themselves convicted by at least one item — and framing that conviction as cause for professional gratitude.
points: The Tacky Ten is grounded in Kearney et al.'s 1991 credibility research, offering teachers a research-backed self-audit for behaviors that erode student trust.
Adolescents are developmentally the most sensitive age group to condescension, making condescending mannerisms one of the highest-stakes credibility risks for secondary teachers.
Sarcasm is dangerous in classrooms because it is ambiguous language; when aimed at a whole room it is statistically guaranteed to be received negatively by at least some students.
Moving test dates damages credibility only when done habitually or for poor reasons — context and communication determine whether the move helps or hurts.
The Tacky Ten works as a PLC discussion protocol precisely because honest teachers recognize themselves in at least one item, opening the door to growth-oriented reflection.
quotes: It's critical to reflect on the idea that humiliation and offense-taking are subjective. Just because I don't intend to offend or humiliate a student doesn't mean students don't experience this in my room. They do. It's an inevitable outcome of the many thousands of interactions that comprise a school year.

There are some teachers that can pull off calling teenagers honey or sweetie. But there aren't many. And I'm not one of them. There is no age range in human development that is more sensitive to condescension than adolescence.

sarcasm is ambiguous language and ambiguous language aimed at a whole classroom is guaranteed to be received incorrectly by at least a few students. This can cause needless offense, alienation, or embarrassment for students.
Moving test dates only hurts your Credibility, in my view, when you're constantly doing it or you're doing it because you don't manage time well.
The solution approach here is to grade fewer things and to simplify that grading as much as possible.
I've never met an honest teacher who's not convicted by at least one item on this list. And to me, that's good news. I'm thankful to have a job where I can continue to improve.
